<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: Second, Justice Kavanaugh closes out his opinion with a long argument for why this decision is needed in the context of sports. He suggests the nature of competition, the spirit of fair play, and the country's deep obsession with sports all require this opinion.\18\ Although he does not explicitly state it, the strong suggestion is that the B.P.J. interpretation of Title IX is limited to the world of sports. The Sotomayor dissent takes the baton from the Kavanaugh opinion and makes this contextual interpretation more explicit:
\18\Id. at 27-29.
[T]here are plenty of contexts outside of athletics in
which Title IX applies and does not allow sex
distinctions like this one to be drawn. . . I do not
understand the majority to suggest, for instance, that
schools could expressly bar transgender students from
participating in certain classes or extracurricular
activities entirely, or on the more extreme end, that
schools could expel transgender students because they
are transgender, and that those actions would not
violate Title IX. Such actions would qualify as sex
discrimination. . .\19\
\19\Id. at 32-33 (Sotomayor, J., dissenting).
Both Justice Kavanaugh (implicitly) and Justice Sotomayor
(explicitly) suggest in the Title IX context, B.P.J. is strictly limited to sports. The opinions leave little doubt that a Title IX case arguing discrimination on the basis of gender identity in an educational context other than sports would be easily distinguishable from B.P.J.
It is the Court's suggestion that its decision is limited to sports that is the more insidious rationale for H.R. 8781. Had the Supreme Court held that Title IX offered no protection from discrimination on the basis of gender identity whatsoever, we doubt the Committee would have considered this bill. But, by inferring its decision in B.P.J. was limited to the context of sports, and by not striking down the holding of Bostock, the Court did not limit transgender rights consistent with the Majority's desires, making H.R. 8781 necessary. Reading the bill in the context of Justice Sotomayor's dissent, it is clear that the Majority would like to prevent Title IX from offering protections to transgender students in those other ``contexts outside of athletics'' she mentioned. This is consistent with the President's Executive Order on Gender Ideology Extremism, which seeks to eliminate transgender individuals from consideration in federal law.\20\ The Majority has justified spending valuable Committee and House Floor time over the last two Congresses on anti-transgender legislation because they needed to protect women's and girls' sports from transgender athletes. Now that the Supreme Court has done just that, H.R. 8781 makes clear the real goal all along was to ensure civil rights law did not protect transgender students on the basis of their gender identity.
\20\Exec. Order 14168, 90 Fed. Reg. 8615 (Jan. 30, 2025).
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING MARKUP OF H.R. 8781
Committee Democrats offered no Amendments to H.R. 8781.
CONCLUSION
The Majority's obsession with making the world harder for transgender students wherever possible appears to be the most important policy goal for this Committee. To achieve this, H.R. 8781 takes legal interpretive power from states and localities, in an attempt to unilaterally mandate a position the Supreme Court did not take, namely that Title IX does not protect students from discrimination on the basis of their gender identity. We disagree. For the reasons stated above, all Committee Democrats present opposed H.R. 8781 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on July 21, 2026. We urge the House of Representatives to do the same.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
Suzanne Bonamici,
Mark DeSaulnier,
Adelita Grijalva,
Members of Congress.
